Alienation

/ay-lee-uh-NAY-shuhn/ - rhymes with nation · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Alienation means a feeling of being isolated or estranged from other people or from one's own work.

After the scandal, the senator confessed to friends a deep alienation from the hometown voters he had known all his life.

Worked Example

When the village market went cashless, the elderly weaver kept her stall but lost her place: customers tapped their phones and drifted off without a word, and the morning gossip she had traded in for forty years dried up. Surrounded by familiar faces, she felt a quiet alienation from the square she had worked since girlhood.

Alienation is more precise than loneliness here because the weaver is not short of company — the square is full. What she has lost is the sense of belonging to it: alienation names the feeling of being made a stranger to people, places, or work that once felt like your own.

How Alienation Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

estrangement

estrangement: a relationship actually broken off, not just a felt distance

disconnection

disconnection: a milder, more matter-of-fact loss of contact

Antonyms

belonging

belonging: the settled feeling of being at home among others

connection

connection: a live bond with people or with one's work

How Strong Is It? — unease → loneliness → alienation → estrangement

unease vs. alienation

unease vs. alienation: Unease is only a vague discomfort in a situation; alienation goes further — a settled sense that you no longer belong to it at all.

loneliness vs. alienation

loneliness vs. alienation: Loneliness is the ache of missing company, curable by a friend's visit; alienation can survive a crowded room, because it is belonging, not company, that has failed.

estrangement vs. alienation

estrangement vs. alienation: Estrangement goes further than alienation: the alienated worker still shows up feeling like a stranger, while estranged relatives have actually broken off contact.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — alien

Root — alien: belonging to another; foreign

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: state or process of

Put it together

Put it together: Alien (belonging to another) + -ation (state of) = the state of having become a stranger. Latin alienus meant 'belonging to someone else,' so alienation is literally the condition of finding that your work, your town, or your circle has stopped being yours.

Use the root in a new word: inalienable

Use the root in a new word: inalienable: The charter calls liberty an inalienable right — one that cannot be handed over or taken away.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / academic

Alienation is the heavyweight term for feeling like a stranger where you should belong — sociologists use it for workers cut off from their own labor. Unlike seclusion, which is chosen and may be restful, alienation happens to you and hurts. If you only mean missing people, say loneliness.
